newsitem.title: USA: A small family-run oil co has big troubles.
newsitem.headline: A small family-run oil co has big troubles.

text.p: While America's oil refining industry has been battered by poor earnings and consolidation for years, one small family-run firm has had more than its share of troubles.

Owned and managed by the Rosenbergs, a wealthy Baltimore family known for its philanthropic gestures, Crown Central Petroleum Corp. had recorded years of losses before turning a small profit in the first quarter of 1997.
Plenty of other U.S. oil refiners have lost money in recent years, but Crown more than most has accumulated a long list of troubles.
It has been embroiled for over a year in a bitter labour dispute that has involved a "lock-out" of unionized employees.

On the environmental front, Crown has a record significantly worse than its peers. It has been penalised hundreds of thousands of dollars for regulatory violations and is being targeted for a lawsuit by environmentalists.
And late last year, in support of a union dispute at Crown's refinery in Pasadena, Tex., the AFL-CIO put the company on its official "boycott" list.

"I don't know of any other company that is being boycotted or that has the kind of wrestling matches they do," said Alvin D. Silber, an oil and gas analyst for brokerage Herzog, Heine, Geduld in New York.
"And I don't know any other company that has such severe problems in the labour arena," Silber said.

For the past 16 months, Crown has been deadlocked in negotiations with workers at its Pasadena refinery, locking out some 250 workers. The lock-out occurred after talks broke down over a company proposal to save $2.5 million in labour costs that included layoffs.
The union's case that the company bargained in bad faith and followed unfair labour practices was thrown out by a regional National Labour Relations Board.
But despite that victory, some analysts criticise Crown for its heavy-handed management style and say it has contributed to the company's poor financial performance.
Over the course of last year, Crown's American Stock Exchange-listed shares dropped around 46 percent. On June 18, Crown stock was trading at $15.25.
"There are real problems in management of the company because of the heavy hand of the family," said an industry analyst who requested anonymity.
Run by Henry, Edward and Frank Rosenberg, Crown can boast a long history in the oil world -- its chief executives are descendents of Amoco's founder, Louis Blaustein.

But it is doubtful whether a family-run oil concern can survive in today's oil world of increasingly large corporations and environmental regulatory expenses, industry analysts contend. Some see Crown as a target for takeover, particularly its refining sector, which showed a $2.5 million net loss in the first quarter of 1997.

"Crown would definitely entertain offers in light of the difficult industry conditions and consolidation. They have been struggling in Houston with the Pasadena refinery," said analyst William D. Hyler of Oppenheimer & Co.

But taking over Pasadena, or its smaller Tyler, Texas, facility could be more of a headache than it is worth. Union workers argue that both plants have been mismanaged and the plants have had a history of costly environmental problems.
"If management obtained subcontracting, even then they could not begin to compensate for losses by mismanagement," said Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union representative Richard Miller.

In the past six years Texas environmental authorities have fined Pasadena four times. "The fact that there have been four enforcement penalties in six years is not a good indication," said Texas Natural Resources Conservation Commission spokesman Terry Hadley. "This is more than a typical refiner."
Last month, a coalition of environmental groups and citizens threatened to sue Crown for allegedly polluting the environment.

Crown's top executive declined an interview request, though a Crown spokesman did stress that the Pasadena refinery won the National Petroleum Refiners Association's award for improvements in safety in 1995 and 1996.
Crown spokesman Joe Coale added the recent NLRB decision throwing out the union case of unfair labour practices at Pasadena shows Crown management has acted fairly and properly.
